title: The King Who Gathered Seven Hundred Songs

title_i18n.en: The King Who Gathered Seven Hundred Songs

subtitle: In Pratishthana’s halls, a Satavahana king gathers the songs of many hearts.
figure: King Hala and the Sattasai Poets
era: Hala tradition c. 1st century CE; anthology redaction c. 2nd-4th century CE
region: Pratishthana and the Maharashtri Prakrit literary world
moral: A court becomes great when it listens to many voices.

sources.citation: Peter Khoroche and Herman Tieken, Poems on Life and Love in Ancient India: Hala's Sattasai (SUNY, 2009)
sources.note: Modern English translation and introduction to the anthology.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent study of Prakrit literary culture and Satavahana language politics.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (University of California Press, 2006)
sources.note: Context for vernacular and cosmopolitan literary economies.

panels.shot: majestic frontal wide of the king on a stone terrace above the Godavari valley at dusk

dialogue.text: In the age of the Satavahanas, King Hala of Pratishthana is remembered not for conquests, but for gathering seven hundred Prakrit songs of love and life.

panels.shot: broad establishing aerial of the Deccan plateau and Godavari river basin

dialogue.text: From the first centuries of the Common Era, Satavahana power stretches across the Deccan, binding river valleys, caravan routes and villages in a changing world of trade and faith.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of Pratishthana city walls and gates bustling with activity

dialogue.text: At Pratishthana on the Godavari, the Satavahana capital hums with merchants from the coast, monks from cave monasteries, and farmers whose seasons drive the kingdom’s pulse.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of the king seated on a simple but dignified throne amid advisors

dialogue.text: Satavahana kings rule by balancing land grants, caravan taxes and religious patronage. Amid them is Hala, remembered in later tradition as a ruler who turned his ear to everyday speech.

panels.shot: slow push-in on the king’s thoughtful profile as Sanskrit and Prakrit texts lie before him

dialogue.text: In his age, Sanskrit grows as the language of gods and royal display. Yet Prakrit—the speech of markets and fields—carries the everyday music of desire, quarrel and teasing.

panels.shot: intimate interior wide of a small court gathering with village women and bards before the king

dialogue.text: Later memory places Hala at the center of an unusual court. Here, not only polished Brahmins but farmers’ daughters and wandering singers can release brief, sharp verses in Prakrit.

panels.shot: medium on the king leaning forward to listen to a woman poet reciting

dialogue.speaker: king_hala_and_the_sattasai_poets
dialogue.text: Speak as you do in the fields and courtyards. Do not polish your tongue for me.

panels.shot: tight shot of a palm-leaf being inscribed by a court scribe with the king observing

dialogue.text: Tradition names Hala as the collector of seven hundred gāthās. Modern scholars see a slow anthology: many poets, many decades, later redactors shaping what his name came to represent.

panels.shot: cross-cut montage wide showing countryside scenes that match different poems while the king studies

dialogue.text: The Gaha Sattasai holds brief flashes of life: a girl mocking her timid lover, a wife angry at a husband’s delay, a farmer’s daughter measuring desire against duty and gossip.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king smiling slightly as a mischievous poem is recited

dialogue.text: Many verses speak in women’s voices, teasing and direct about desire and frustration. In this imagined court, a king nods as the propriety of elite halls bends toward the candor of courtyards.

panels.shot: low-angle interior showing Brahmin scholars debating before the king

dialogue.text: Around Hala’s name later gather debates on language. Can Prakrit, the ‘speech of snakes’ in some eyes, rise beside Sanskrit? The anthology quietly answers by enduring in royal memory.

panels.shot: close-up of the king’s hand placing the Prakrit manuscript among other royal treasures

dialogue.text: Whether or not he chose each verse, the Hala tradition signals this: a Satavahana court counts short Prakrit love songs among its treasured instruments of prestige and identity.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide of scribes copying the anthology over generations

dialogue.text: Across the second to fourth centuries and beyond, redactors and scribes reshape the anthology. New poems enter, some fall away, yet the frame of Hala’s seven hundred songs remains.

panels.shot: medium shot of a Gupta-era court poet reading from the Sattasai

dialogue.text: By the early centuries of the Gupta age, Maharashtri Prakrit is firmly linked with romance. Poets across regions draw on Hala’s anthology as they shape their own courtly lyrics.

panels.shot: wide of Bana in his study with manuscripts, including one labeled by a small emblem of Hala

dialogue.text: By the seventh century, Bana’s words show that Hala’s Sattasai is known in the north. The anthology travels, remembered as a Satavahana king’s legacy of brief, piercing gāthās.

panels.shot: scholarly close-up of a modern researcher examining a fragile palm-leaf in a library

dialogue.text: Today, scholars read through layers of manuscript and memory, careful not to credit all seven hundred verses to one hand, yet tracing how a royal name anchors a many-voiced tradition.

panels.shot: contemplative medium shot of King Hala on the terrace at night, stars above, distant village lights below

dialogue.text: Hala’s story reminds us: a court becomes truly great when it gathers and preserves the speech of many lives, letting even brief village songs echo alongside the proclamations of kings.
